How a Mechanical Pencil Clutch Advances Lead

A mechanical pencil holds its lead in a clutch, called a collet in the patent described here. Each press of the button carries the lead forward by a small step, and on release the collet grips the lead again.

At a glance

Gripping part
A collet with split jaws made of spring material
What clamps it
A tapered receiver tube, acting through rolling balls
Each press
Advances the lead by a small step
Design described
US4521126A, a patent titled Mechanical pencil
Caveat

The clutch that grips the lead

The mechanism described here comes from a patent for a mechanical pencil. The gripping part is a collet with split jaws made of spring material. Left alone, the jaws tend to spring open, away from the lead. A receiver tube with a tapered guide face works with the collet, and rolling balls sit between the two. In the normal position, a wedging action among the collet, the receiver tube and the balls clamps the jaws on the lead and holds it firmly for writing. Exact construction varies by pencil design.

Sources: [1]

What one press does

In the patent, when the button is operated, the receiver tube and the collet advance together toward the tip, with the lead still gripped, until the receiver tube stops against the tip piece. Pushing farther lets the receiver tube spring back at once on its own, while a pusher drives the collet on toward the tip piece, where the collet is fully opened. When the button is released, springs return the pusher and the collet, and the retracted collet firmly grasps the lead again. The lead has advanced by a small step instead of sliding freely.

The patent describes a fault in earlier pencils of this kind. An opened chuck was likely to close first and then retract, so the small length of lead just pushed out could be pulled back into the pencil and lost. Returning the receiver tube separately is the patent's answer. Its drawings show a button that slides along a slot in the casing, and the text says a general type of push button on the rear end of the casing may be used instead.

Sources: [1]

A second strip lays the parts out in order. Close-up panels show the texture of the graphite lead, the jaws gripping the lead, the spring, the plastic barrel threads and wear marks on the nose cone tip.

Its four-step strip reads: press button, clutch opens, lead slides forward, release and clutch grips. The captions say the knock rod moves rearward and pulls the clutch jaws open, and that the spring then pushes the rod forward so the clutch closes. The patent describes the directions differently. Its pusher moves forward toward the tip to open the collet, and springs carry the parts back when the button is released.

A materials panel lists graphite lead, a stainless or brass clutch, a molded plastic barrel, a rubber eraser and spring steel. A last panel, marked as examples to observe only, compares a good grip, where the lead is held firmly, with a worn clutch that lets the lead slip under light pressure and a broken fragment in the clutch that blocks movement.

How Bioluminescent Plankton Makes Waves Glow

Some dinoflagellates, a kind of microscopic plankton, give off blue light when breaking waves or other water motion disturb them. Not every bloom glows. It depends on which organisms are present.

At a glance

What glows
Certain dinoflagellates, a kind of microscopic plankton
Trigger
Disturbance by waves or other movement in the water
Color of light
Neon blue
Southern California species
Lingulaulax polyedra, 35 to 60 micrometers across
Best viewing
A dark beach at least two hours after sunset
Suggested purpose
Scientists think it startles or confuses predators

What makes the water flash

Red tides occur when microscopic plankton called dinoflagellates multiply rapidly and form dense blooms that can discolor the water. At night, when the cells of some species are disturbed by waves or other movement in the water, they emit a neon-blue glow that can be seen with the naked eye. The Scripps Institution of Oceanography says scientists think the light is a predator-avoidance mechanism that startles or confuses organisms that might eat the plankton.

The infographic lays this out as a sequence: calm water, a paddle or stir disturbance, a breaking wave, a bright flash and a quick fade. Its cell panel shows mechanical shear from wave action leading to light emission from a single magnified dinoflagellate.

Sources: [1]

Which blooms glow

Not every bloom or red tide glows. Scripps says bioluminescence occurs only when certain species of dinoflagellates or other organisms are present. In Southern California the species most often responsible is Lingulaulax polyedra, formerly named Lingulodinium polyedra. Each cell measures 35 to 60 micrometers across and contains pigments that give it a reddish-brown color. On sunny days the cells swim toward the surface, where they concentrate and intensify the coloration of the water.

Another bloom-forming dinoflagellate common in Southern California waters, Prorocentrum micans, is non-toxic and non-luminescent, but it can still contribute to red tide events.

Sources: [1]

When it is easiest to see

During a red tide dominated by light-producing species, Scripps says the displays are best seen from a dark beach at least two hours after sunset. Visibility is not guaranteed, because these events are unpredictable and vary in intensity and location. The infographic gives its own conditions for a brighter glow: dark water with less ambient light, stronger turbulence in the wave wash, and a bloom with many cells near the surface.

Sources: [1]

Glowing water and safety

A red tide is not the same thing as a harmful algal bloom. Many red tides are relatively harmless, while others can cause harm through toxin production or other mechanisms, depending on the species present. Scripps says most red tides along the California coast are not considered dangerous to humans, but they can sometimes cause skin or eye irritation or respiratory discomfort. Off the coast of Washington, glowing blooms have been linked to Alexandrium catenella, which produces the neurotoxin saxitoxin, and those blooms are often harmful.

The infographic carries a similar caution, that not all glowing water is safe, and adds that some harmful algae blooms do not glow. It shows the glow being watched from the beach edge at a respectful distance, without entering the surf.

Sources: [1]

How Retroreflective Sign Vinyl Sends Headlights Back

Retroreflective sign sheeting contains tiny glass beads or cube-corner reflectors that send much of a headlight's light back toward its source. The sign does not glow on its own. It looks bright to a driver whose eyes are close to the headlights.

At a glance

What it is
Sheeting applied to the face of a traffic sign
Reflecting elements
Microscopic glass beads or cube-corner reflectors
What it does
Sends much of the incoming light back toward its source
Brightest when
The driver's eyes are close to the headlights
Own light
None; it does not glow by itself

Scattered light and returned light

Most objects reflect light. The most common kind is diffuse reflection, in which light scatters after striking a rough surface such as trees, clothing or carpet. Only a very small amount of that scattered light reflects back toward the light source.

Retroreflection is the ability of a surface to reflect light back toward the light source. Retroreflectivity is the measurable property of a material's ability to redirect light back to its source. The infographic draws the same contrast. Its comparison panel shows ordinary matte vinyl scattering light in many directions and retroreflective vinyl returning light in a narrow cone toward the source. It also states that the material does not glow by itself and that it returns much of the incoming light toward the source.

Sources: [1]

Inside the sheeting

To make a sign retroreflective, sign manufacturers apply sheeting to its face. The sheeting contains either microscopic glass beads or cube-corner reflectors. The Minnesota Department of Transportation's Signs 101 manual says that if every bead and cube corner could be made perfectly shaped, all the reflected light would return directly to the headlights. Real sheeting does not have perfectly shaped lenses.

The infographic shows the sheeting as a stack of layers: a clear protective face film, a colored translucent film, a retroreflective layer of microprismatic cube corners or glass beads, a pressure-sensitive adhesive and an aluminum substrate. Its light-path strip follows the light in order. Headlights approach the sign, light enters the sign face, light refracts and reflects inside the retroreflective layer, light exits and returns toward the source, and the driver sees a bright sign. Close-up panels show cube corners, embedded glass beads and a sign surface sparkling under headlights at night. A sign-shop panel shows a reflective vinyl roll, an aluminum sign blank, a felt squeegee, a release liner and test swatches under a hand light.

Sources: [1]

Why the driver's position matters

Drivers see more reflected light the closer their eyes are to the headlights. The manual calls the angle formed between the headlights, the sign and the driver's eyes the observation angle. The smaller that angle, the higher the retroreflectivity. Retroreflective materials are also more efficient when the light source is approximately perpendicular to the sign face, which is why the manual says it is important to orient signs to face approaching traffic.

Sources: [1]

Why signs use it

The manual says the MN MUTCD requires traffic signs to be either retroreflective or illuminated, so that they show the same shape and color both day and night. Because making a sign retroreflective is more cost effective than illuminating it, retroreflective sheeting is used on all signs. The manual also notes that some signs may look almost new during the day but be completely ineffective at night, a problem that is usually a function of the type and age of the retroreflective material.

Sources: [1]

How a Heat Dome Works

A heat dome occurs when a persistent region of high pressure traps heat over an area. It can linger for days to weeks while the sun makes conditions on the ground progressively hotter.

At a glance

What it is
A persistent region of high pressure that traps heat over an area
How long it lasts
Days to weeks
Linked to
The behavior of the jet stream, a band of fast-moving winds high in the atmosphere
In cities
Pavement, buildings and other hard surfaces absorb and retain more heat
Not literal
There is no physical dome or glass lid

High pressure that stays in place

A heat dome occurs when a persistent region of high pressure traps heat over a particular area, according to NOAA. It can linger for days to weeks. Descending air can warm, and the resulting weather pattern can keep very hot conditions in place. Air descending down mountains can also contribute to a heat dome, as it warms even more.

A heat dome is not a literal glass dome. The infographic states that heat domes are not physical domes or glass lids. It describes them as areas of high pressure with sinking air and weak mixing that allow heat to build and persist.

Sources: [1]

The jet stream's part

Heat domes are typically linked to the behavior of the jet stream, a band of fast-moving winds high in the atmosphere that moves in meandering, wavelike patterns. When the jet stream meanders north, it moves slower and can sink, which lowers humidity. This allows the sun to create progressively hotter conditions on the ground.

The infographic shows the jet stream arching around the area of high pressure, with cooler air and storms on either side. NOAA's article reports that during a heat wave in June 2023, storms formed along the edge of a ridge of high pressure. A meteorologist quoted there said such storms are sometimes called ridge-riding storms.

Sources: [1]

How the heat builds near the ground

The infographic lays out the build-up as a chain. A strong area of high pressure parks over a region. Air sinks, compresses and warms. The jet stream arches around the high and steers storms away. Sinking air keeps clouds from forming, so strong sunlight heats the ground, buildings and water every day. With less vertical mixing, warm air lingers near the surface. Dry soil and hot surfaces then release stored heat, which makes the next day hotter.

Its timeline runs from sunny, hot weather at the start, through drying soil and pavement that stores heat, to dangerous heat stress and warm nights. NOAA's article adds a point about cities. Because of the heat island effect, temperatures there are generally higher than in surrounding rural areas, since dense concentrations of pavement, buildings and other hard surfaces tend to absorb and retain more heat.

Sources: [1]

Warm nights and the June 2023 heat wave

NOAA's article was written during a heat wave that affected more than 50 million people across the southern U.S. and Mexico in June 2023, brought on by what it calls a heat dome. Overnight temperatures were expected to be abnormally warm and to give little to no relief. The Weather Prediction Center said there might be more danger than in a typical heat event, because of the longevity of near-record or record high nighttime lows and elevated heat index readings.

According to the weather service, heat causes more deaths across the United States each year than any other weather event, including tornadoes, floods and hurricanes. The infographic's side panel lists reasons the heat feels worse: high humidity slows the evaporation of sweat, pavement and buildings store heat, nights stay warm so bodies and homes cannot recover, and the longer the pattern stalls, the more heat accumulates.

Sources: [1]

How Comb Jellies Make Traveling Rainbow Light

Comb jellies are oval, gelatinous sea animals that swim by beating eight rows of tiny comblike plates. As the plates move, they break up light into a shimmering rainbow, an optical effect that is distinct from light an animal produces itself.

At a glance

Body

Rainbow effect

Diet

Eight rows of beating combs

The Monterey Bay Aquarium describes the comb jelly as an oval-shaped animal with eight rows of tiny comblike plates that it beats to move through the water. Its soft body is thin skin stretched over a body composed of more than 95 percent water, with no bones or shells to weigh it down. The infographic labels the plates as fused cilia plates, or ctenes, and shows the comb rows on a transparent body.

Sources: [1]

Where the rainbow comes from

As a comb jelly swims, its comb rows break up light and produce a shimmering rainbow effect. The beating cilia split incoming light into colors. This is an optical effect, and it is distinct from biologically produced light.

The infographic lays out the light path step by step. White aquarium light hits the moving plates, and diffraction and interference separate the colors. As the cilia beat, the shimmering bands travel. The animal itself remains mostly transparent. A comparison panel sets this shimmer, caused by external white light scattering from moving plates, against true bioluminescent blue-green light, which it describes as produced by an internal chemical reaction in other marine animals. The infographic calls the rainbow effect mostly structural light scattering from moving cilia.

Sources: [1]

A predator made mostly of water

Comb jellies are voracious predators. The aquarium lists their diet as plankton, small crustaceans and other jellies, and says some species can expand their stomachs to capture other jellies half their own size. The infographic shows trailing tentacles and labels their colloblasts as prey-catching cells.

The aquarium describes a jelly as a gelatinous creature with few specialized organs. Many jelly species have a gravity-sensitive structure called a statocyst that helps with orientation in the water, and the infographic marks a statocyst on its cutaway. Comb jellies belong to the phylum Ctenophora. Relatives listed by the aquarium include the sea gooseberry, the lobed comb jelly and the bloody-belly comb jelly. Their ecosystem is the open ocean, and range and size vary with species.

How Frost Flowers Grow on Young Sea Ice

Frost flowers are delicate ice crystals, not plants. They form when water vapor turns straight to solid ice on young sea ice in cold, calm conditions, and they become salty by interacting with brine.

At a glance

What they are
Ice crystals, not plants and not alive
Where they form
On the surface of young sea ice
How they form
Water vapor becomes solid ice without first turning into liquid water
Conditions
Cold and calm
Why they are salty
They interact with brine
Effect on the ice
They roughen the surface and dramatically affect its electromagnetic signal

Crystals grown from vapor

Frost flowers are ice crystals, not plants or living things. The National Snow and Ice Data Center defines them as crystals of ice that form when water vapor becomes a solid, bypassing the liquid phase, and deposits itself on the sea ice surface. The center's glossary adds that frost flowers roughen that surface and dramatically affect its electromagnetic signal.

They form over young sea ice in cold, calm conditions. They are produced by vapor gradients over the ice, and their salt comes from interaction with brine.

Sources: [1]

The process the infographic lays out

The infographic shows a slab of young sea ice, labeled new, thin and dark, resting on relatively warmer ocean water under very cold air. Brine channels, described as salty water in microscopic veins, run through the ice, and a very salty film sits on its surface. What thermal runaway is

A Federal Aviation Administration report, a summary of its studies of lithium cells in aircraft cargo compartments, describes thermal runaway as a chemical reaction within a cell that results in a dramatic, uncontrolled rise in temperature and pressure. As the temperature rises, pressure inside the cell increases and activates its pressure-relief ports, releasing the electrolyte. How Basalt Columns Crack Into Polygons

Basalt columns form when a cooling lava flow contracts and fractures. The cracks advance inward from the cooling surfaces and divide the rock into columns, most of them hexagonal.

Cooling, contraction and cracks

Columnar jointing consists of sets of regularly spaced, parallel fractures, called joints, that intersect in a roughly prismatic pattern. The National Park Service gives the cause as a short chain: cooling causes contraction, which in turn causes fracturing. The fractures propagate from the top and bottom of a flow inward toward the center, dividing the cooling body into columns.

The jointing forms after a lava flow or other igneous body has solidified, but while it is still at high to medium temperature. It is thought to form during rapid cooling. The developing fracture system is thought to let fluids circulate, which can further hasten the cooling.

The infographic follows the same order in stages: hot lava is emplaced, the boundaries lose heat first, contraction builds tensile stress, cracks meet in a polygon network, and crack tips advance inward as cooling continues, leaving columns.

Why the columns are polygons

Most columns are hexagonal, but they may have anywhere from three to seven sides. The predominantly hexagonal pattern arises because contractional stress is most efficiently relieved by three fractures that intersect at angles of 120 degrees, which creates six-sided polygons. The infographic's caption notes that the columns are not perfect hexagons.

Columns are oriented perpendicular to the main cooling surfaces of lava flows and other igneous bodies. The infographic illustrates this with a top surface, a bottom surface and a sloped surface: where heat leaves, cracks form at right angles to that surface. It also states that basalt columns are intact rock bounded by joints, not single crystals or growth structures.

Irregular joints and other rocks

Some lava flows have irregular columnar jointing known as entablature, typically found in the interior portion or near the top of a flow. Its irregular fracturing is likely due to a different cooling rate in the flow's interior. The infographic makes a comparison of its own, between ordered columnar joints and irregular blocky joints, which it says are formed by cooling, weathering or unloading.

Columnar jointing is most commonly found in basaltic lava flows. It also occurs in lava flows of other compositions, pyroclastic flow deposits, some lava domes, volcanic necks and some shallow intrusions.

Devils Postpile National Monument has columns up to 60 ft (18 m) long, in a basalt flow up to 400 ft (122 m) thick that pooled after it erupted approximately 100,000 years ago. How Magnetotactic Bacteria Follow Earth’s Magnetic Field

Magnetotactic bacteria live in water and sediment and carry a chain of tiny crystals of magnetic iron minerals. The chain works like an internal compass, aligning the swimming cell with Earth's magnetic field.

At a glance

What they are
Aquatic or sediment-dwelling microorganisms
Compass parts
Magnetosomes, each a membrane-wrapped crystal of a magnetic iron mineral
Minerals
Magnetite or greigite
Crystal size

Flagella

Toward their preferred oxygen concentration

A compass built from crystals

A magnetosome is a tiny crystal of a magnetic iron mineral with a membrane around it. Early studies indicated that the membrane contains phospholipids and proteins. A mature magnetosome holds a single crystal of magnetite or greigite, with a shape and size that depend on the species, mostly between 30 and 100 nm. A review published by the American Society for Microbiology notes that the number, size, shape, arrangement and chemical composition of the crystals vary considerably between groups of these bacteria.

In the two Magnetospirillum species the review concentrates on, the crystals are cuboctahedral magnetite, about 45 nm in size when mature. The infographic draws magnetite and greigite crystals as octahedrons and labels that a common shape. Its scale panel gives its own approximate sizes for a sediment grain, a bacterium and a crystal, and its crystal range is narrower than the review's.

Sources: [1]

Why the crystals form a chain

The force on a single magnetosome in Earth's magnetic field is too weak to align a cell effectively. Stacked into a line, the magnetosomes add their magnetic moments together and form a much stronger magnetic dipole, strong enough to align the whole cell with the rather weak geomagnetic field, much as a compass needle is aligned. The review says the findings suggest this alignment is a passive, physical effect.

The infographic states the same idea in steps: iron is stored as orderly magnetosome crystals, the crystal chain gains a combined magnetic moment, and the swimming cell tends to align with the local geomagnetic field. It also states that proteins help position and hold the magnetosomes in a straight chain.

Sources: [1]

Alignment is not the whole trip

All magnetotactic bacteria characterized so far use flagella to swim. Lining up with the field reduces three-dimensional trial-and-error swimming to movement along a line. Together with responses to chemicals such as oxygen, this guides the bacteria efficiently to their preferred oxygen concentration in layered environments. The infographic separates the jobs: magnetic alignment for orientation, flagella for movement, and chemical or oxygen sensing for choosing a favorable zone. Its sediment jar shows oxygen-rich water above, a low-oxygen transition zone, and oxygen-poor sediment below.

The infographic cautions that the bacteria do not simply always swim north, and that behavior varies with species, habitat and hemisphere. The review gives some background. In early studies, cells exposed to a magnetic field seemed to prefer one direction along it over the other. In Earth's northern hemisphere predominantly north-seeking cells were isolated, and in the southern hemisphere predominantly south-seeking cells. The review says it is not currently understood exactly how this swimming polarity is controlled.

How Trees Pull Water Upward

Water rises through a tree as a passive process. Evaporation from the leaves creates tension in the water-carrying xylem, and because water molecules hold together, that pull draws a connected column of water up from the roots.

Transpiration, the evaporation of water at the leaf surface

The pull starts in the leaves

Transpiration is the loss of water from a plant through evaporation at the leaf surface, and it is the main driver of water movement in the xylem. Inside the leaf, water on the surface of the cells evaporates into the air spaces. That lowers the water potential and increases the tension on the water in the xylem. At the leaf surface the negative pressure is equivalent to –2 MPa, a value that varies greatly. It can be negligible at high relative humidity and substantial at low relative humidity.

Water moves from where water potential is higher to where it is lower. For water to travel from the soil to the air, the potential must fall at each stage, from soil to root, stem, leaf and atmosphere. The OpenStax biology textbook describes transpiration as a passive process in which metabolic energy in the form of ATP is not required for water movement. The infographic makes a statement of its own, that roots do not mechanically pump water to the canopy.

Why the column holds together

The cohesion of water molecules to each other helps keep the water column connected, so the pull from the leaves can draw water upward from the roots. The textbook says that at night, when stomata shut and transpiration stops, the water is held in the stem and leaf by the adhesion of water to the cell walls of the xylem vessels and tracheids and by cohesion. This is called the cohesion-tension theory of sap ascent.

The infographic lays out the route in order: soil water enters fine roots, water moves into the xylem, cohesion holds the narrow columns, evaporation from moist leaf-cell walls creates tension, and water vapor diffuses through open stomata. Its xylem panel labels vessels as wide conduits and tracheids as narrow conduits.

Each stoma on the leaf surface is surrounded by two guard cells, which open and close in response to cues such as light, leaf water status and carbon dioxide. Transpiration is regulated primarily through this opening and closing. When stomata are open, water vapor is lost, and up to 90 percent of the water taken up by roots may be lost through transpiration.

The textbook says stomata shut at night and transpiration stops. The infographic shows stomata mostly closed at night, with lower evaporation and weaker tension, and mostly open in the daytime, with higher evaporation and stronger tension.

The formation of gas bubbles in the xylem, called cavitation, interrupts the continuous stream of water from the base to the top of the plant. The break in flow is termed an embolism. Dragline silk from orb-weaving spiders changes its mechanical behavior with humidity. Wet dragline fibers can supercontract: they shorten when free to move and develop a contraction stress when held in place.

What supercontraction means

Humidity changes the mechanical behavior of dragline silk. Wet dragline fibers can supercontract. A fiber that is free to move shortens. A fiber that is restrained develops a contraction stress instead. The magnitude varies among species and silk types. The infographic states that strong supercontraction is characteristic of many orb-weaver dragline silks, and that other web silks generally show little to modest supercontraction.

Sources: [1]

What the measurements found

A study in the Biophysical Journal by Vehoff and colleagues quantified the effect of relative humidity on dragline silk from two spiders, Nephila clavipes and Nephila senegalensis. The analysis is based on 126 single fiber measurements. The shape of the stress-strain curve varied significantly with humidity. Below 35% relative humidity the curve consisted of two linear regimes. Above 75% it took an elastomeric shape.

The strain at which a fiber broke rose with humidity in a linear way, predicting an extensibility range from 13% to 42% for spider dragline silk. The elastic modulus fell as humidity rose. The breaking force varied little with humidity. The authors conclude that the influence of humidity is sufficient to explain the great range of mechanical properties reported for the silk in the literature.

Sources: [1]

Water inside the fiber

X-ray fiber diffraction points to a composite structure in the silk: beta-sheet crystallites embedded in an amorphous matrix. The study's authors write that water can easily permeate the fiber and is incorporated in the amorphous matrix. They assume that this hydration interferes with hydrogen bonds between the amorphous chains, which leads to a loss of rigidity. Weighing measurements that the authors call very preliminary indicate that almost two-thirds of the fiber mass at full hydration is due to water uptake.

The infographic lays out a sequence in stages built on the same structure. In a dry fiber under tension, the chains are stretched, and hydrogen bonds and other interactions hold the structure in place. Water molecules diffuse into the amorphous regions. Some interactions are disrupted and the chains move more freely. The chains then relax into new positions and the fiber shortens, often reversibly. The infographic labels this a simplified model, not a universal one.

How a Gravitational-Wave Detector Hears Spacetime

A ground-based gravitational-wave detector such as LIGO is an L-shaped laser interferometer. It sends laser light down two perpendicular arms, recombines the returning beams, and reads tiny changes in the arm lengths as changes in the interference signal.

The basic interferometer

LIGO describes its detectors as, at their cores, Michelson interferometers. Each is L-shaped with two equal-length arms. A beam splitter sends laser light along the perpendicular arms. The returning beams are recombined, producing an interference signal that responds to tiny differences in their optical path lengths.

LIGO's arms are 4 km (2.5 mi) long, and LIGO says its interferometers are by far the largest ever built. The instrument has to measure a change in distance 1,000 times smaller than a proton, which is why it must be larger and more sensitive than any interferometer built before.

Sources: [1]

Making the arms act longer

As simple Michelson interferometers, instruments with 4 km arms would still be too short to detect gravitational waves. LIGO places an additional mirror in each arm near the beam splitter, 4 km from the mirror at the end of the arm. The space between them is a Fabry Perot cavity. The laser in each arm bounces between the two mirrors about 300 times before it is merged with the beam from the other arm. That increases the effective distance each laser travels from 4 km to about 1200 km and builds up the laser light within the interferometer, both of which increase sensitivity.

Sources: [1]

Building up laser power

The laser first enters the interferometer with a power of about 40 Watts, but the instrument needs to operate closer to 750 kW. Power recycling mirrors make up the difference. They continually reflect laser light that has already traveled through the instrument back into the interferometer. The added power sharpens the interference fringes that appear when the two beams are superimposed. Signal recycling mirrors further enhance the signal received by the photodetector, and the interferometers were built with mechanisms to damp out unwanted vibrations, or noise.

Seawater that meets magma

Hydrothermal vents form where seawater meets magma. NOAA describes them as hot springs produced by underwater volcanoes at spreading ridges and convergent plate boundaries. Seawater percolates down through fissures in the ocean crust, the cold water is heated by hot magma, and it reemerges to form the vents. Seawater in hydrothermal vents may reach temperatures of over 700° Fahrenheit. It does not boil because of the extreme pressure at the depths where vents form.

The infographic's cutaway shows the same loop. Cold seawater infiltrates fractures in the ocean crust, is heated near a shallow magma heat source, and rises as buoyant vent fluid. The cutaway labels a water-rock reaction in which metals and reduced sulfur enter the fluid.

A venting black smoker emits jets of particle-laden fluid. The particles are predominantly very fine-grained sulfide minerals, formed when the hot hydrothermal fluid mixes with near-freezing seawater. The minerals solidify as they cool and build up chimney-like structures. Black smokers are chimneys formed from deposits of iron sulfide, which is black. The infographic labels the dark plume as particle-rich, not smoke or lava.

The infographic lays out growth in stages. Hot fluid rises from a bare fissure. A porous, anhydrite-rich mound forms where the fluid meets sulfate-bearing seawater. A narrow conduit focuses the flow, and sulfide minerals deposit on its walls, thickening the chimney and building it upward and outward. Continued deposition makes branching spires. An older chimney may fracture, and new vents form on its flanks. A separate panel shows mineral layers becoming brittle, a blocked conduit redirecting the flow, a wall collapsing, and growth resuming from side vents.

Leader, streamer and return stroke

Most lightning starts inside a thunderstorm and travels through the cloud. In the most common type of cloud-to-ground lightning, a channel of negative charge called a stepped leader zigzags downward in roughly 50-yard segments in a forked pattern. NOAA's National Severe Storms Laboratory says the leader is invisible to the human eye and shoots to the ground in less time than it takes to blink.

As it nears the ground, the stepped leader causes streamer channels of positive charge to reach upward, normally from taller objects in the area, such as a tree, house or telephone pole. When a leader and a streamer connect, a powerful electrical current begins flowing. This return stroke, the bright part, travels about 60,000 miles per second back toward the cloud along the existing channel.

A negative cloud-to-ground flash consists of one or perhaps as many as 20 return strokes. Lightning flickers when the process rapidly repeats itself several times along the same path. The channel that carries the current is one to two inches in diameter, surrounded by a region of charged particles.

The infographic states that its dimensions and brightness are exaggerated for explanation. How Honeybees Map a Flower Patch

A honey bee's waggle dance works like a set of directions to a flower patch. The angle of the waggle run on the comb gives the direction relative to the sun, and a longer run stands for a longer flight.

Turning the comb into a compass

The angle of a returning bee's waggle run conveys direction relative to the sun. NC State Extension gives examples. If the food source lies directly away from the sun, the straight run points vertically down. If the food source is 60 degrees to the left of the sun, the waggle run is 60 degrees to the left of vertical.

The infographic's sun compass panel shows the rule with three labels: toward the sun is up on the comb, away from the sun is down on the comb, and an angled run keeps the same offset from the sun. How Lightning Makes Fulgurites

A fulgurite is a tube of glass made when lightning passes through sand. The discharge melts sand around its path, and the melt cools into glass that keeps some of the shape of the route.

Sand melted by lightning

A lightning discharge through suitable sand can briefly melt material around its path. The melt cools into a glassy fulgurite that preserves some of the shape of the route the discharge took. At Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve, the National Park Service describes fulgurites as blackish tubes of glass.

The Park Service gives lightning a temperature of 50,000 degrees F, hotter than the surface of the sun. It says the bolt vaporizes the area where it shoots through the sand and melts the surrounding sand into dark glass.

The infographic lays out the formation in order: a dry dune, attachment of the lightning, a current path through the sand, local melting, rapid quenching and, later, exposure. Its cutaway labels a hollow tube with a glassy wall, fused grains, vesicles, mineral inclusions and a sand-coated exterior. A grain-scale panel shows separate grains before the strike, a transient melt during it, and quenched glass bridges after.

Why no single shape

Fulgurite form and composition vary with lightning energy, current path, moisture, grain size, mineralogy and cooling, and not every strike makes one. The infographic shows the current path branching where moisture, minerals, pore space and grain contact vary. It shows different results in different materials: branching tubes in sand, massive forms in soil and a thin glassy coating on rock.

It also shows what happens afterward. A buried fulgurite is fragile. Shifting sand exposes it, it breaks into segments, and the pieces become rounded fragments. Fulgur is the Latin word for lightning. Cicero used the expression condere fulmina, meaning to dig up thunderbolts, which the Park Service says indicates that early Romans had knowledge of fulgurite formation in sandy areas of Italy.

At Great Sand Dunes, the presence of fulgurites in the sand is a reminder that lightning can and does strike the exposed dunefield during storms. The Park Service asks visitors who find one to study and enjoy it but leave it in the sand for the next visitor.

How Mantis Shrimp Read Polarized Light

Mantis shrimp can detect the polarization of light, which is how light waves are oriented, not their color. University of Queensland researchers reported in 2008 that the animals they studied could see both linear and circular polarized light.

Seeing how light is oriented

Polarization describes how light waves are oriented, not their color. People notice the effect of linear polarization through polarized sunglasses, which cut out glare, and use circular polarization in things such as 3D glasses for movies and filters for cameras.

University of Queensland researchers found that the mantis shrimp they studied could distinguish both linear and circular polarization. The university described the ability to see circular polarized light as a completely new type of vision. Professor Justin Marshall, of its School of Biomedical Sciences and the Queensland Brain Institute, said the animal has a very small brain but one of the world's most complex visual systems, with 12 color channels where humans have three. The research was published in Current Biology.

Marshall said only the males have the ability, which implies it has something to do with sex. He said it is probably a secret communication channel between males and females that keeps predators from knowing what is going on.

Inside a Hydrothermal Vent Chimney

A hydrothermal vent chimney grows where hot, mineral-rich fluid from the ocean crust meets cold seawater. As the fluid cools, minerals precipitate into chimney walls and sometimes a dark plume.

At a glance

Fluid source
Seawater that percolates into the ocean crust and is heated by hot magma
Temperature

Seawater's loop through the crust

Hydrothermal vents are the result of seawater percolating down through fissures in the ocean crust near spreading centers or subduction zones. The cold seawater is heated by hot magma and reemerges to form the vents. Hot seawater circulating through the crust carries dissolved minerals. It may reach temperatures of over 700° Fahrenheit, and it does not boil because of the extreme pressure at the depths where vents form.

The infographic draws this loop as a descent of cold seawater through fractured crust, heating and a water-rock reaction at depth, and a buoyant upflow of hot fluid through the active conduit in the middle of the chimney. Its pressure panel says that under great depth pressure, very hot fluid can remain liquid.

Where hot fluid meets cold seawater

When the vent fluid cools against seawater, minerals precipitate, forming a chimney and sometimes a dark plume. NOAA describes a venting black smoker as emitting jets of particle-laden fluid, in which the particles are predominantly very fine-grained sulfide minerals formed when the hot hydrothermal fluid mixes with near-freezing seawater. Black smokers are chimneys formed from deposits of iron sulfide, which is black. White smokers are formed from deposits of barium, calcium and silicon, which are white.

The infographic marks this meeting as a mixing front at the top of the chimney, with hot vent fluid on one side and a particle plume on the other.

Sources: [1]

Layers of the chimney wall

The infographic shows growth in stages: a hot-fluid jet, an anhydrite scaffold of calcium sulfate, a porous young wall of sulfide deposits, a chalcopyrite-rich lining of copper-iron sulfide, outer zones of sphalerite and iron sulfides, and a branched chimney with sealed and new conduits. Its magnified wall section runs from the hot conduit through a chalcopyrite-rich inner lining and mixed-sulfide zones to an iron-sulfide exterior, with anhydrite remnants, porous channels and cold seawater in cracks. It marks the zones as variable.

The archive note for the picture credits a Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution feature, The birth of a black smoker, for the anhydrite scaffold, the chalcopyrite lining, the sulfide zoning and the wall porosity. Those details are not on the NOAA page.

Life on chemical energy

Scientists first discovered hydrothermal vents in 1977 near the Galapagos Islands, and found them surrounded by large numbers of organisms that had never been seen before. These biological communities depend on chemical processes that result from the interaction of seawater and hot magma.

The infographic places the life at the zones where vent fluid and seawater mix. It labels the central jet as the hottest part and uninhabited, with microbial films on mixing interfaces, tubeworms in an oxygenated zone, mussels at diffuse flow, and shrimp and crabs near chemical gradients. Its pathway panel shows microbes using chemical energy, not sunlight. An accuracy note on the picture says field conditions vary, including temperature, mineralogy, flow, microbes, animals and chimney architecture.

Lord Howe Island Phasmid — Survival on Ball's Pyramid

A large, flightless stick insect

The Lord Howe Island phasmid, Dryococelus australis, is a large, flightless stick insect. The New South Wales listing document gives adult males as reaching 120 mm, more commonly 106 mm, and adult females as reaching 150 mm, more commonly 120 mm.

The infographic shows a female and a male side by side, with the label wingless, and a life cycle strip running from egg to hatchling, nymph, final molt and adult. A comparison panel titled body form varies sets the wingless phasmid beside a generic winged stick insect.

Lost from Lord Howe Island

The phasmid was once very common on Lord Howe Island, common enough to be used as bait for fishing. It became extinct there soon after a supply ship ran aground in 1918 and the ship rat came ashore with the cargo. The species was considered extinct until live individuals were discovered on Ball's Pyramid in 2001.

The infographic tells that history in three pictures: the former range on Lord Howe Island, a disappearance it attributes to introduced rats, and the rediscovery on Ball's Pyramid.

One site on Ball's Pyramid

In the wild the phasmid is known only from a single site on Ball's Pyramid, a rocky outcrop 23 km south east of Lord Howe Island. The insects have been reported only from within a foraging area considered to be 30 m x 6 m. Melaleuca howeana is likely the only host plant for the phasmid at that site.

The listing document estimates the wild population as extremely low, with fewer than 50 mature individuals. This very restricted range is central to the insect's conservation status. The infographic marks the refuge as a narrow band on the rock and labels the status critically endangered under the Australian EPBC Act, with the words exceptionally restricted wild range.

In 2003, two pairs of phasmids were collected from Ball's Pyramid and a captive breeding program was started. The listing document, citing a July 2011 communication, reports 800 adults in captivity producing viable eggs.
